title: Nachiketa turns down Death's gifts
hookLine: Death offers a boy gold, horses, long life and heaven's music, and the boy says keep them
carry: vairagya: the wanting doesn't own you
tomorrow: three roads open: action, devotion, knowledge. which one first?

lines: GOLD, HORSES, LONG LIFE, HEAVEN'S MUSIC.
cards: A boy named Nachiketa has waited three days at the door of Death. Yama, the lord of death, was away, and when he returns, ashamed to have left a guest hungry, he grants three wishes.
For the third, Nachiketa asks the hardest thing: what happens after we die? Yama tries to buy him off. Take sons and grandsons who'll live a hundred years, he says.
Cattle, elephants, gold, horses. Rule the earth. Live as long as you like.
Take these heavenly women with their chariots and music; no mortal could win them. Just don't ask me that.

teach.b: Nachiketa answers, in the Katha Upanishad: these won't last past tomorrow. Keep your horses, keep your songs. No one is made happy by wealth.
And he holds out for the teaching, and that refusal is why Yama teaches him.

teach.h: NO THIRST FOR THINGS SEEN OR HEARD OF.
teach.b: That's vairagya, non-attachment, the second wing, and Patanjali's thread fifteen describes it: the mastery of one who no longer thirsts for things seen, or things heard about.

Seen means this world: the praise, the paycheck, the last slice of cake. Heard about, says the commentary, includes heaven itself. Yama's heavenly music was exactly that, a reward you'd only heard of.
Even spiritual prizes can become one more thing to crave.
Patanjali's word for the result is vashikara: mastery, being in charge of the pull. Nachiketa didn't stop wanting.
Thread sixteen goes to the root: from knowing the seer comes freedom from thirst for everything nature is woven of.
In Hindu teaching this isn't only for monks; householders are taught to hold money, success, even religious rewards loosely.
Look back at the week: open hands for a teacher, a drunk monkey and a still lake, two birds, a self awake through sleep, two wings, a star that never moves, and a boy who said no thanks to Death.

how: In Hindu teaching, vairagya is not only for monks: householders are taught to hold wealth, family and even religious rewards loosely, and the Yoga Sutras' opening chapter is often studied as a complete short course in meditation.

o: loosening the pull of what you want
a calm feeling after deep meditation
hating pleasure and giving it all up

games.q: the boy, Death and the second wing — tap the pairs.
p: the lord of death, who offered them
mastery: the pull doesn't own you

s: for Patanjali, non-attachment means you can never enjoy anything
it's vashikara, mastery: the thing no longer owns you.
Nachiketa took Yama's gold and horses, then asked his question anyway
he said keep them; they won't last past tomorrow. he wanted the truth.
the higher non-attachment comes from knowing the seer
thread sixteen: from knowing purusha, no thirst even for the gunas.

games.q: you've heard serious meditators reach perfect calm, and you want it badly. what would Patanjali and Nachiketa say?
o: it's one more pull, a thing heard about. want the truth, not the prize.
keep craving until you get it.
games.why: thread fifteen names things seen and things heard of, even heaven. Nachiketa turned down heaven's music to hear the truth.

practice: Let one pull come to mind, something you've tasted and want again, or something you've only heard about and want anyway, and notice where you feel it: the chest, the stomach, the hands.
Loosen your grip by one finger, then another; you don't have to give the thing up, only notice the wanting doesn't have to own you.
If you pray, offer the wanting to God, the way many Hindus offer food before they eat it, so it comes back as prasad; if you don't, say quietly, i can enjoy this without it owning me.

wordCard.voice: Vairagya, non-attachment: mastery of the pull of what you've tasted and what you've only heard of. Nachiketa kept wanting one thing, the truth, and let the rest go.

orig.note: Sanskrit: non-attachment, dispassion; from vi + raga, without coloring or passion.

carryVoice: Your line: vairagya, the wanting doesn't own you. Nachiketa said keep your horses. That's the week, and day three hundred one.

sources.ref: Yoga Sutra 1.15 (non-attachment toward things seen and heard of; vashikara)
Vyasa's commentary on 1.15 (heavenly rewards among things 'heard of')

Katha Upanishad 1.1.20–1.1.29 (Nachiketa's third wish; Yama's offers of long-lived sons, cattle, elephants, gold, horses, land, long life and heavenly women with chariots and music; 'these last only till tomorrow… keep your horses, your dance and song'; 'no one is satisfied by wealth')
